issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance of an immovable-property agreement is not automatically entitled to succeed merely because it was filed within the limitation period and time was not expressly made essential; the court must consider the agreed timeline, the parties’ conduct, and the surrounding circumstances in deciding whether to grant the discretionary remedy.
material_facts: The agreement required the buyer to complete specified steps, including paying the balance and arranging the sale documents, within a stated period.
The buyer took no steps to complete the transaction for more than two and a half years and produced no contemporaneous communication supporting his claim that he had repeatedly sought completion.
The buyer had paid only a small part of the agreed consideration and did not tender the balance or arrange the sale documents within the stated period.
The buyer purchased other properties during the period of inactivity.
The value of the urban property rose substantially between the agreement and the buyer’s demand for completion.
The Supreme Court rejected the buyer’s explanation for his inaction and concluded that the delay, together with the rise in value, made specific performance inequitable.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the decree granting specific performance was set aside, and the trial court’s decree was restored. The buyer’s prolonged inaction, considered with the contractual timeline and the substantial rise in property values, made specific performance inequitable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10 and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary and must be exercised on sound judicial principles; Sections 21 and 23 address compensation and the effect of a stipulated sum. Section 55 of the Contract Act distinguishes the consequences of failure to perform when time is or is not essential, and Article 54 of the Limitation Act prescribes the period for filing a specific-performance suit. The absence of an essential-time term and filing within limitation do not make the contractual time limits irrelevant or compel a decree. Under Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, even where time is not essential, performance must occur within a reasonable time assessed in light of the contract, the property, and surrounding circumstances. Satyanarayana v. Yellogi Rao explains that delay alone is insufficient without conduct or neglect that prejudices the defendant or makes relief inequitable; here, prolonged inaction coupled with a substantial rise in property values created that inequity. Jiwan Lal was distinguished because the delay there had a reason, while the contrary approach attributed to S. V. Sankaraninga Nadar was not accepted insofar as it excluded rising prices from the discretionary assessment.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and immovable_property_sale_agreement and agreement_set_completion_period and buyer_inactive_beyond_completion_period and buyer_did_not_tender_balance_or_prepare_sale_documents and no_credible_reason_for_inactivity and property_value_rose_substantially

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: A party appealed a decree granting specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_agreement: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property.
predicates.agreement_set_completion_period: The parties specified a period for completing the transaction and taking steps toward completion.
predicates.buyer_inactive_beyond_completion_period: The buyer took no meaningful steps to complete the transaction after the agreed completion period expired.
predicates.buyer_did_not_tender_balance_or_prepare_: The buyer neither tendered the remaining consideration nor arranged the documents needed to complete the sale during the relevant period.
predicates.no_credible_reason_for_inactivity: The court rejected the buyer’s explanation for failing to act during the period of inaction.
predicates.property_value_rose_substantially: The property’s value increased substantially while the buyer remained inactive.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a specific-performance decree for an immovable-property sale, the agreement sets a completion period, the buyer remains inactive without a credible reason and does not take completion steps, and the property rises substantially in value, the rule yields denial of specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee’s purchase of property after a trial-court decree refusing specific performance, even with knowledge of the litigation, does not by itself establish that the plaintiff is entitled to an equitable preference over the transferee.
material_facts: The trial court refused specific performance and ordered repayment of the earnest money.
After that decree, a third party purchased the property with knowledge that litigation was ongoing.
The original sellers also appealed the decree, so the dispute was not being contested only by the subsequent purchaser.
The plaintiff had paid only a small part of the agreed consideration.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to hold that the equities favored the plaintiff alone merely because the subsequent purchaser knew of the litigation and acquired the property after the trial-court decree.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the claimed equities in light of the subsequent purchase, the purchaser’s knowledge of the litigation, the continued participation of the original sellers in the appeal, and the small proportion of the consideration paid by the plaintiff. It did not treat the purchaser’s knowledge of litigation as sufficient, by itself, to confer an equitable preference on the plaintiff.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and transferee_bought_after_trial_court_refused_specific_performance and transferee_knew_of_litigation and original_sellers_also_appealed and plaintiff_paid_only_a_small_part

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: A party appealed a decree in a dispute over specific performance.
predicates.transferee_bought_after_trial_court_refu: A transferee acquired the property after the trial court had refused the plaintiff specific performance.
predicates.transferee_knew_of_litigation: The transferee knew that litigation concerning the property was ongoing when acquiring it.
predicates.original_sellers_also_appealed: The original sellers also pursued an appeal concerning the decree.
predicates.plaintiff_paid_only_a_small_part: The plaintiff had paid only a small part of the agreed consideration.

issues.definition: When a transferee acquires the property after specific performance was refused, knows of the litigation, the original sellers also appeal, and the plaintiff has paid only a small part of the consideration, the plaintiff does not receive an automatic equitable preference.
